title: Continuation Betting Strategy for Canadian Poker Players
excerpt: The continuation bet is the most common play in online poker and the most misused. Here is how Canadian players should size, select and stop c-betting.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Raise before the flop, bet after the flop. It is the most frequently executed sequence in online poker, and for a lot of Canadian players it is close to automatic. That automation is exactly the problem. Continuation betting became standard advice in an era when opponents folded far too often, and the modern player pool has adjusted. Continuation betting strategy today is less about whether to fire and much more about choosing the right boards, the right sizing and the right moments to check instead. Get those three things right and the c-bet remains the most profitable tool you own. Keep firing on autopilot and it becomes the fastest way to bleed a bankroll one small pot at a time.

What a continuation bet actually accomplishes

When you raise preflop, you tell the table you have a strong range. When you bet the flop, you follow through on that story. A c-bet works because it does several things at once: it wins pots outright when your opponent misses, it charges draws to continue, it builds the pot when you are ahead, and it denies free cards to hands that would improve past you.

The key insight is that you do not need a good hand to have a good c-bet. What you need is a range advantage, and the two are not the same thing. If the board is one that connects far better with your preflop raising range than with your opponent's calling range, betting is profitable across most of your holdings, including the ones that missed completely.

Board texture is the whole game

The single biggest improvement most players can make is to stop asking whether they hit the flop and start asking who the flop favours.

Boards where you should bet often

  • High and dry. Something like ace-seven-two rainbow. Your raising range is packed with aces and big cards; the caller's range is not. Bet nearly every hand you hold.
  • King or queen high with disconnected low cards. Similar logic. You hold the top pairs and the overpairs far more often than your opponent does.
  • Paired low boards. Neither player connects often, but you represent the overpairs credibly and your opponent has to fold a great deal.

Boards where you should slow down

  • Middling and connected. Nine-eight-seven with two of a suit. This texture smashes a calling range full of suited connectors and small pairs while missing your big cards entirely.
  • Low paired boards against a calling station. The range logic still holds, but it does not matter if your opponent never folds.
  • Monotone flops. Three of a suit dramatically shrinks how often opponents fold, and your bluffs have less equity when called.
  • Boards that hit the caller's range specifically. Against a player who defends the big blind with a wide, low-card-heavy range, a flop of six-five-four is their board, not yours.

Sizing: small, large, or nothing

Modern continuation betting uses two distinct sizes for two distinct purposes, and the old habit of firing two-thirds pot on every flop leaves money on the table.

The small bet

Roughly a quarter to a third of the pot, used on boards where you have a large range advantage. You are betting a very wide portion of your range, so you do not need much fold equity per hand to profit. The small size risks less, gets called by worse hands more often, and lets you continue applying pressure cheaply on later streets. Dry ace-high boards are the classic home for this size.

The large bet

Two-thirds pot up to full pot, used on boards where you have a nut advantage rather than a range advantage, and where equities run close. Think of a board where you hold the sets and top two pair far more often than your opponent, but where their draws have real equity. You want to charge those draws and build a pot you intend to keep betting.

The check

Checking is not a failure to c-bet. On boards that favour your opponent, checking protects your entire range, keeps weaker hands in the pot against your marginal made hands, and sets up profitable turn play. Players who never check with strong hands become trivially easy to read, because their check always means weakness and observant opponents will attack it relentlessly.

Adjusting to Canadian online games

Strategy in a vacuum is only half the picture. Who is sitting across from you matters enormously, and the games available to Canadians vary considerably in quality depending on where you play.

Regulated Ontario tables sit in shared liquidity pools with a broad mix of recreational and serious players, and the tougher regulars in those games will punish a player who c-bets every flop. Against them, board selection and mixed frequencies genuinely matter. Our 888poker Ontario review covers what the game selection actually looks like for players in the province.

Softer games, wherever you find them, call for a cruder and more profitable approach. Against opponents who call too much, cut your bluffs sharply and bet bigger with value hands. Against opponents who fold too much, fire relentlessly regardless of texture. Exploitative play beats balanced play whenever your read is correct, and identifying which kind of table you are on is worth more than any amount of theory. Our guide to online poker for Canadian players covers game formats and where the softer pools tend to be found.

The turn is where c-bets go wrong

Most losses attributed to over-c-betting actually happen on the turn. A player fires the flop with nothing, gets called, then fires again out of stubbornness on a card that changed nothing about the situation.

The discipline to check back or check-fold the turn after a called flop bet is worth more than any refinement to your flop strategy. Ask a simple question before every second barrel: what specific hands that called the flop are folding to this bet on this card? If you cannot name them, do not bet. Good turn barrels come on cards that genuinely improve your range or credibly scare theirs, not on every card that fails to complete a draw.

A practical checklist

  • Ask who the board favours before asking what you hold.
  • Use a small size on dry, range-advantaged boards and a large size on high-equity boards where you hold the nuts more often.
  • Build a checking range that includes strong hands, so your checks are not automatically read as weakness.
  • Name the folding hands before firing a second barrel.
  • Adjust hard for opponent tendencies rather than defaulting to theory.

None of this is complicated, but all of it requires thinking rather than reflex. The c-bet is still the most profitable play in poker. It just stopped being free. For more on protecting your roll while you develop these habits, keep an eye on our poker guides and news.
